chunks: "I'd start by pinning down three things: how many bits the ADC has, what the low and high reference voltages are, and whether the code is unsigned.
Say it's a 12-bit ADC with the reference at the 3. 3 volts supply and ground as the low end, and I read 3000. Each code is worth the full range divided by 2 to the N , so 3.
3 over 4096, which is 0. 806 millivolts. The voltage is the code times that: 3000 times 0. 806 millivolts is 2. 417 volts.
In general it's V equals V low plus code times (V high-V low) over 2 to the N , so if the ADC's reference range were 0. 5 to 3. 3 volts, I'd add the 0.
5 volts offset and scale by 2. 8 volts instead. Two things I'd flag. Some datasheets divide by 2 to the N-1 so that the top code reads exactly V ref ; the difference is 0.
024%, so about 0. 6 millivolts here. And that's the voltage at the pin. If there's a divider in front, say 200 k over 100 k to measure a battery, I multiply back by 3.
Also, if the reference is just the supply, the reading is only as accurate as that supply, so I'd calibrate it or use an internal reference."
